title: Rites hold us
hookLine: burial, cremation, Tibetan sky burial: each tradition's rite carries its own meaning

cards: Early morning on a high hillside in Tibet. A body, wrapped in cloth, is carried up to a flat place among the rocks. Monks have chanted.
A man whose work this is prepares the body. Family members may watch from a distance, or go home. Then, out of a wide sky, the vultures come down.

To someone from far away, it can look shocking. To the people who keep this rite, it carries a meaning of its own: the body is no longer needed, and so it is given, one last time, to living creatures.

teach.b: First, the earth. In the Bible, God tells Adam: "for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return."

Jewish and Muslim traditions call for burying the body in the ground, traditionally soon after death, simply and with care. Christian burial carries the hope of resurrection, and some Christians choose cremation.
The grave says: the body goes back to where it came from.
Second, the fire. Hindu and Sikh families traditionally cremate.

In Hindu understanding the fire returns the body to the elements and frees the one who lived in it; a close family member, by tradition a son, lights the pyre. The fire says: what was here is released. Third, the birds.
In Tibetan Buddhist understanding, consciousness has already left the body, so what remains is an empty vessel.
Offering it to the vultures is a final act of generosity, feeding other beings, and a plain lesson in impermanence for those who watch.
In Tibetan it's called jhator, giving alms to the birds. The sky says: even this can be given. Fourth, what they share.

teach.h: SOMETHING FOR THE HANDS TO DO
teach.b: Each rite gives the mourners something to do with their hands at the moment they least know what to do: shovel the earth, carry the body, light the fire, walk up the hill.
It tells them where to stand, what to say, who goes first. When nobody can think, the rite does some of the thinking.
Different rites, each belonging to its people, and in each of them, rites hold us.

how: Funeral rites differ by tradition: Jewish and Muslim burial soon after death, Christian burial or cremation, Hindu and Sikh cremation, and in parts of Tibet sky burial, each carried out by the family and community in its own way.

games.why: the rite holds everyone there, guests too: it tells you where to stand and what to do, if you let it.

practice: Choose a tradition's funeral rite, one different from the one you grew up with, or your own if you've never looked at it closely, and gather what you already know: who washes the body, who carries it, what is said, and by whom.
Notice, too, what you don't know. Then hold the people who keep that rite with respect, the way you'd want your own held.
